_help.about: Fire is fuel (design 30 Sept §AX). Every campfire has a store that burns down: flames -> low -> embers -> out. Fuel is gathered from the world (dead wood, brush, reeds, dung, peat, driftwood) and dropped on the fire. What a biome offers decides whether a camp there can live. Restart after editing.
_help.fire: store_max_units: the most a fire holds. burn_scale: units burnt per real minute at full flame is 1/kind.burn_min, times this. low_share: below this share of store the fire reads 'low'. embers_min: real minutes the embers stay relightable after the store hits zero. tended_burn_scale: burn rate while folk are alive at the fire; the camp loop (§BL, CampSim) feeds it from the woodpile. Note from Mike's play on 30 Sept: before the loop existed every camp fire was out by day 14 and no flame was left in the world to light a torch at — a save from before the loop stays dark; start a new world. A dead tended fire is relit by its folk at dawn from the woodpile (they keep an ember). relight: how a dead fire comes back. light_radius_m: the safe / dread-draining radius (§BA). old_hearth_units: the charred branches left in a cold old hearth (OldHearths; Claude Code's default 2, written here 2 Oct as PROGRESS asked). Design §CN: they count as the hearth's fuel, but it still needs kindling laid before the torch's swing lights it.
_help.wet: Fuel gathered in rain or from soaked ground: burn-time multiplier and the chance it lights at all.
_help.kinds: burn_min: real minutes one unit burns at full flame. heat: warmth/light scale (brush burns hot and fast). smoke: visual smoke scale. carry_items: burden slots one unit takes.
_help.biomes: Per biome key (BiomeTemplates names): fuel kinds on offer with an abundance 0-1 that scales how much the gather pass places. An empty block means nothing burns there: a camp there dies.
_help.kindling: (design §CN) A cold fire needs kindling. Embers still come back with an armful of dry fuel (§AX; embers_need_kindling false). A fire that is fully out (a campfire, an old hearth, a delve's brazier in delves.json fire_holders) must be laid before the torch's swing (torch.json swing) will light it: laid_fire.kindling_items of kindling and at least laid_fire.fuel_units_min of fuel; an old hearth's charred branches (fire.old_hearth_units) count as its fuel. Lay it with right click (lay: interact), the way fuel is fed (§AX). catch: a swing lights a laid fire when its kindling is dry. Kindling gathered or left out in rain is wet until it dries (fuel.json wet.dry_h_game; under a roof it stays dry), and wet kindling takes only if its kind is wet_ok (catch_wet >= wet_threshold): otherwise it smokes and stays cold. No dice roll, nothing to mash. How fast the flame takes: time_s_max x (1 - catch_dry or catch_wet). Kindling with no fuel flares for its burn_s and goes out. kinds: real materials only, each with its sources; an id that is also a fuel kind (grass_bundle, reeds) is that same carried item (fuel_kind true). gather: litter (picked up), plant / fungus / lichen (taken from a living or dead one of its genera), ground, animal. biomes: what is fine and dry where you are, likeliest first; filled per biome family by parallel agents on 2 Oct. A kind tied to genera is listed only where those genera grow in the biome's plant file (§CA). Gate: tools/kindling_check.py (0 errors before commit). _stopgap: biomes whose lists are only core kinds until their family's fill lands (the tropical forests, 2 Oct).

reeds.from: Last year's dead reed stems, snapped at the water's edge.
reeds.notes: A quick, hot flash: good to start a fire, gone in moments.

dry_twigs.notes: Slower to catch than bark or grass, but it carries the flame up into the fuel.

dead_leaves.name: Dry leaves
dead_leaves.from: Crisp dead leaves from under broadleaf trees, taken from the top of the litter where it is driest.
dead_leaves.notes: Catches fast and burns out faster; a damp leaf only smokes.

conifer_needles.name: Dead conifer needles
conifer_needles.from: Brown needles gathered from under pines and other conifers, or from dead lower twigs.
conifer_needles.notes: Resin in the needles makes them flare. Found only where conifers grow.

birch_bark.name: Birch bark
birch_bark.from: Peeled in curls from dead birch logs, or the loose curls on living trees, then shredded fine.
birch_bark.notes: Its oils keep water out: it lights even when damp, and wet bark wipes dry.

bogwood_splinters.name: Bog-wood splinters
bogwood_splinters.from: Old pine roots and trunks dug out of the peat while cutting turf, dried and split into thin splinters.
bogwood_splinters.notes: Old pine kept in the peat and still full of resin; people dried the splinters by the fire and burned them for light.

casuarina_needles.name: Casuarina needles
casuarina_needles.from: The fallen, needle-like twiglets that carpet the sand under ironwood (she-oak) trees, raked up by the handful.
casuarina_needles.notes: Not a pine, but its litter is raked up for cooking fires along Asian coasts.

cattail_down.name: Cattail down
cattail_down.from: Pulled from a ripe cattail head, which breaks open into a big wad of fluff.
cattail_down.notes: Flashes almost at once; feed it grass or reeds straight away or the flame dies.

cedar_bark.name: Shredded cedar or juniper bark
cedar_bark.from: Stringy bark torn from juniper, cypress or redcedar trunks, then rubbed between the palms into a loose nest.
cedar_bark.notes: The classic tinder of the dry American West and the Pacific coast. It shreds fine but drinks rain.

chaga.name: Chaga
chaga.from: Broken from the black, cracked growths on birch trunks; the black crust is knocked off and the brown inside is what takes fire.
chaga.notes: Scored as flame kindling: it takes a spark or ember well but a flame poorly, and flames only briefly. Once lit it smoulders slowly and holds its ember, which is why it was used to carry fire.
sources: Karst, Amanda (2010), Conservation Value of the North American Boreal Forest from an Ethnobotanical Perspective (Convention on Biological Diversity), p. 25 (Inonotus obliquus, cinder conk: 'Tinder for transporting fire'): https://www.cbd.int/doc/external/report-ethnobotany-en.pdf

coconut_husk.name: Coconut husk fibre
coconut_husk.from: Torn from the dry brown husk of an old fallen coconut and teased into a loose nest of fibres.
coconut_husk.notes: The tinder of tropical shores. A smouldering husk keeps mosquitoes away.
sources: FM 21-76 US Army Survival Manual (1992), Appendix B, 'Coconut': 'Dried husk fiber is an excellent tinder. A smoldering husk helps to repel mosquitoes.' (as reproduced at https://www.wilderness-survival.net/Appb.php)

cottonwood_bark.from: Stringy inner bark pulled from dead and fallen cottonwoods, then rubbed into a loose nest.
cottonwood_bark.notes: Dead and fallen cottonwoods are common along rivers, so it is easy to find. The Northern Cheyenne also used dry, rotted cottonwood wood as tinder.

dead_bracken.name: Dead bracken
dead_bracken.from: Brown dead fronds snapped from last year's bracken; fronds still standing are the driest.
dead_bracken.season: late autumn to spring, once the fronds have died brown
dead_bracken.notes: Dead bracken stands dry through winter and is a known fire hazard; once rained on it is as useless as wet grass.

driftwood_shavings.name: Driftwood shavings
driftwood_shavings.from: Curls and splinters scraped from sun-dried driftwood lying above the high-tide line.
driftwood_shavings.notes: Inuit saved the dry scrapings from working driftwood to start fires all year.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Driftwood' (Inuit collected and stored dry driftwood scrapings to start fires year-round; driftwood is still used as kindling): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Driftwood

'Inuit knowledge and use of wood resources on the west coast of Nunavik, Canada', Études/Inuit/Studies 37(1), 2013 (the study Wikipedia cites for the scrapings): https://www.erudit.org/en/journals/etudinuit/2013-v37-n1-etudinuit01423/1025259ar.pdf

dry_moss.name: Dry moss
dry_moss.from: Pulled from the top of a moss hummock, mat or log after dry weather, then rubbed fluffy.
dry_moss.notes: Only after a dry spell: moss drinks rain and fog.
sources: Hough, Walter, 'Fire-making Apparatus in the U. S. National Museum' (Smithsonian Institution; Project Gutenberg ed.) -- East Greenland (Angmagsalik): the ember is put 'into dried moss (sphagnum)', blown, 'and soon get a blaze': https://www.gutenberg.org/files/53531/53531-h/53531-h.htm
Wikipedia, 'Qulliq' (lamp wick of cottongrass and/or 'dry moss rubbed between the hands until it is quite inflammable'): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qulliq

Karst, Amanda (2010), Conservation Value of the North American Boreal Forest from an Ethnobotanical Perspective (Convention on Biological Diversity), p. 25 (Sphagnum: 'Fuel for smoking hides, meat'): https://www.cbd.int/doc/external/report-ethnobotany-en.pdf
Wikipedia, 'Qulliq' (Inuit lamp wick 'composed of dry moss rubbed between the hands until it is quite inflammable'): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qulliq

Hough, Walter (1890), 'Fire-making Apparatus in the U.S. National Museum', Report of the U.S. National Museum for 1888, pp. 531-587 -- pp. 547-548, Cherokee: 'The tinder was of a fungus or dried moss'; p. 558, East Greenland: the ember is put 'into dried moss (sphagnum)', blown, 'and soon get a blaze': https://www.gutenberg.org/files/53531/53531-h/53531-h.htm
Jack Raven Bushcraft, 'Other natural tinders' (mosses: 'Dried out, however they can make a useful tinder'): https://www.jackravenbushcraft.co.uk/other-natural-tinders/

dry_sedge.name: Dry saw-sedge
dry_sedge.from: Saw-sedge cut in the fen and left to dry; mind the leaf edges, they cut like saws.
dry_sedge.season: cut in early spring, then dried
dry_sedge.notes: Cut at Wicken Fen since at least 1414, for thatch and also as fuel and kindling.
sources: National Trust, 'The history of Wicken Fen' ('In early spring, sedge was harvested and dried for use in thatching, but also as a fuel and for kindling'): https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/cambridgeshire/wicken-fen-national-nature-reserve/history-of-wicken-fen
Wikipedia, 'Wicken Fen' (the sedge cut there, first recorded in 1414, is Cladium mariscus): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wicken_Fen

fatwood_shavings.name: Fatwood shavings
fatwood_shavings.from: Shaved from the resin-soaked stump of a dead pine, or from the base of its dead lower branches.
fatwood_shavings.notes: Soaked with resin, it lights even when wet and burns long and hot.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Fatwood' (resin-saturated pine heartwood; 'It lights quickly even when wet'): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fatwood

Kochanski, Mors L., Northern Bushcraft (Lone Pine Publishing, 1988), ch. 1 Firecraft ('The wood at the base of the dead lower branches of pines is usually saturated with resin'; conifer resin is 'the most important fire-lighting material to use with matches in the Northern Forests')

Kirtley, Paul (2019), 'Tactics For Fire-lighting In The Damp, Cold Months' (fatwood is 'similarly moisture-resistant and exceptionally energy-dense'): https://paulkirtley.co.uk/2019/tactics-for-fire-lighting-in-the-damp-cold-months/
Wikipedia, 'Fatwood' (pine heartwood; 'lights quickly even when wet, is very wind resistant'): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fatwood
Wikipedia, 'Tinder' (pitchwood is 'the resinous wood which decays last from dead conifers'): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tinder

Wikipedia, 'Fatwood' (resin-impregnated heartwood of pine stumps; 'It lights quickly even when wet'): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fatwood

fir_pitchwood.name: Douglas-fir pitchwood
fir_pitchwood.from: Chopped and shaved from the pitch-soaked heart of old Douglas-fir stumps and rotted logs.
fir_pitchwood.notes: The pitch-soaked heartwood is the last part of a dead fir to rot, and it does not take up water, so it lights in rain. It is the rainforest's fatwood.
sources: Moore, William R. (1985), 'Nature's Own Conifer Tree Pitch Fire Starter', Mother Earth News ('Douglas fir produces the richest (that is, the most flammable) pitch'; 'about the only way to find Douglas fir pitch is to chop the heartwood out of rotted stumps or logs'): https://www.motherearthnews.com/sustainable-living/nature-and-environment/conifer-tree-pitch-fire-starter-zmaz85ndzgoe/

Wikipedia, 'Tinder' ('Pitchwood is the resinous wood which decays last from dead conifers'; it 'does not absorb water, so it remains easy to ignite in any weather'): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tinder

manuka_bark.name: Mānuka bark
manuka_bark.from: Papery strips peeled from the loose, flaking bark of mānuka or kānuka (older writers called both mānuka).
manuka_bark.notes: Māori travelling in cold weather tied up a bundle of dry mānuka bark and kindled it at one end.
sources: Best, E. (1924) 'The Polynesian method of generating fire', Journal of the Polynesian Society 33(130): 87-102: 'When travelling in cold weather natives sometimes procured a bundle of dry manuka bark, which they put ties round and kindled at one end': https://www.jps.auckland.ac.nz/document//Volume_33_1924/Volume_33,_No._130/The_Polynesian_method_of_generating_fire,_by_Elsdon_Best,_p_87-102/p1 (full text: https://www.folksong.org.nz/pinepine_te_kura/fire_rituals_full.html)

palm_fibre.name: Palm fibre
palm_fibre.from: Fibre pulled from the old leaf bases on a palm trunk, or the brown cloth-like sheath at the crown.
palm_fibre.notes: The leaf bases shelter it, so it is often the driest thing in a wet swamp.
sources: Green Deane, Eat The Weeds, 'Cabbage Palm, Sabal palmetto' ('The boot fiber makes excellent tinder and if one digs some dry tinder can usually be found there even in the rain'): https://www.eattheweeds.com/cabbage-palm-sabal-palmetto/

plant_down.name: Seed down
plant_down.from: Seed fluff of cottongrass, willow catkins or cottonwood, plucked from ripe heads or scooped from drifts.
plant_down.season: summer to autumn, while the white heads last
plant_down.notes: Catches in a blink and is gone as fast: lay twigs on it.
sources: Aiken, S.G. et al. Wikipedia, 'Tinder' (natural tinders include seed fluff from milkweed, dandelions and cottonwood; dead standing goldenrod; pitchwood, which does not absorb water and stays easy to ignite in any weather): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tinder

puffball.name: Dry puffball
puffball.from: An old puffball dried brown where it grew; break it open for the spongy fibres inside.
puffball.notes: It smoulders better than it flames: better at holding a spark than catching a torch.
sources: Burk, W. R. (1983) 'Puffball usages among North American Indians', Journal of Ethnobiology 3(1): 55-62 (Blackfoot: 'puffballs were commonly used as tinder or punk for lighting fires'): https://ethnobiology.org/sites/default/files/pdfs/JoE/3-1/Burk1983.pdf

reindeer_lichen.name: Reindeer lichen
reindeer_lichen.from: Picked from the pale, branching lichen mats on open, dry ground, when they are crisp.
reindeer_lichen.notes: Crisp when dry, spongy when wet. It dries faster than the moss around it, often within a few hours of dew.
sources: Munger, G.T. (2008), 'Cladonia (Cladina) spp.', Fire Effects Information System, USDA Forest Service ('Reindeer lichens dry readily, becoming a highly flammable fuel'): https://www.fs.usda.gov/database/feis/lichens/claspp/all.html

Missouri Department of Conservation field guide, 'Gray reindeer lichen (reindeer moss)' ('When dry, shrubby lichens such as these have been used as tinder for starting fires'): https://mdc.mo.gov/discover-nature/field-guide/gray-reindeer-lichen-reindeer-moss

rockrose_twigs.name: Rockrose twigs
rockrose_twigs.from: Dead twigs snapped from gum rockrose bushes, whose leaves and stems are sticky with resin.
rockrose_twigs.notes: Rockroses give off oils that make them burn easily; they are fire plants whose seeds sprout after a blaze.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Cistus' (species emit volatile oils, rendering the plants flammable; pyrophytes whose seeds survive fire): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cistus

S. E.-A. Henaoui (2018), 'Flammability and Combustibility of Cistus Plant Groups in Tlemcen Region (Algeria)', International Journal of Ecology and Environmental Sciences 44(4): 383-393 (cited by Wikipedia, 'Cistus')
Wikipedia, 'Cistus ladanifer' (the whole plant is covered with a sticky, fragrant resin, labdanum): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cistus_ladanifer

sagebrush_bark.name: Shredded sagebrush bark
sagebrush_bark.from: Pulled in long grey strips from the trunks of old or dead big sagebrush, then rubbed between the hands into a fluffy nest.
sagebrush_bark.notes: The Klamath and Modoc bound it tight into torches to carry fire. The shrub's oils make even green sagebrush wood burn well.
sources: S. A. Barrett (1910), 'The Material Culture of the Klamath Lake and Modoc Indians of Northeastern California and Southern Oregon', University of California Publications in American Archaeology and Ethnology 5(4), p. 257: 'the torch made of tightly bound dry sage-brush bark': https://www.craterlakeinstitute.com/online-library/wp-content/uploads/material-culture-klamath-modoc.pdf

Wikipedia, 'Artemisia tridentata' (used as firewood, the wood's oils being particularly flammable): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemisia_tridentata
Plants For A Future, 'Artemisia tridentata': 'The shredded bark is a fine tinder for starting fires': https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Artemisia+tridentata

Wikipedia, 'Artemisia tridentata' (used as firewood, 'the wood's oils being particularly flammable'): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemisia_tridentata

spanish_moss.name: Spanish moss
spanish_moss.from: Grey strands pulled down from bald cypress and other bottomland trees and teased into a loose ball.
spanish_moss.notes: Native peoples of the South wrapped dry Spanish moss round arrow shafts and lit it to make fire arrows. It drinks rain, so it must be dry.
sources: Immel, Diana L. (2001), USDA NRCS Plant Guide 'Spanish Moss, Tillandsia usneoides' (Houma and Seminole uses; 'Dry Spanish moss was used for fire arrows. Deane, Green, Eat the Weeds, 'Tillandsia usneoides' ('A bundle of stripped moss also makes excellent tinder'): https://www.eattheweeds.com/tag/tillandsia-usneoides/

spruce_twigs.name: Dead spruce twigs
spruce_twigs.from: Thin dead twigs snapped from the bare lower trunk of a spruce, under the green crown.
spruce_twigs.notes: The crown above keeps them dry in rain, and their resin helps them flare: the first place to look in a wet spruce wood.
sources: Kirtley, Paul (2015), 'Northern Forest Fire Lighting Fundamentals' (spruce: 'a mass of small, dead twigs near the base of their trunk'; 'they contain resin and are usually dry due to the protection from dense green foliage above'): https://paulkirtley.co.uk/2015/northern-forest-fire-lighting-fundamentals/

Kirtley, Paul (2019), 'Tactics For Fire-lighting In The Damp, Cold Months' (dead twigs low on the tree are 'remarkably sheltered from precipitation'): https://paulkirtley.co.uk/2019/tactics-for-fire-lighting-in-the-damp-cold-months/
Kochanski, Mors L., Northern Bushcraft (Lone Pine Publishing, 1988), ch. 1 Firecraft ('A small handful of dry spruce branches elbow to finger tip long is broken into thirds')

tola_twigs.name: Dry tola twigs
tola_twigs.from: Fine twigs and scaly leaf-tips snapped from dead tola bushes, the resinous shrubs of the dry puna.
tola_twigs.notes: Tola is the dry puna's firewood. Bolivian bakers and plaster-makers pick it because it burns hot.
sources: Tapia Alejo, C. R. (2022) 'Uso y beneficio de la thola (Parastrephia lepidophylla) en producción sostenible de ecosistemas de altura en Bolivia', Revista de Investigación e Innovación Agropecuaria y de Recursos Naturales 9(2) (a resinous shrub, 0.5-2 m; daily cooking fuel; bakers and plaster kilns (yeseras) prefer supu thola for its stronger burn and heat): http://www.scielo.org.bo/scielo.php?pid=S2409-16182022000200063&script=sci_arttext&tlng=es

tulip_tree_bark.name: Tulip-tree inner bark
tulip_tree_bark.from: Peeled from dead tulip-tree limbs and rubbed between the hands into fine fibres.
tulip_tree_bark.notes: The inner bark of a dead limb breaks down into fine, hair-like fibres that make a ready tinder nest.
sources: Walker, Todd (2015), 'Tulip Poplar: A Rich Resource for Year-Round Wilderness Self-Reliance', Survival Sherpa ('Process the inner bark into fine hair-like fibers to form a tinder bundle'; from a dead limb): https://survivalsherpa.wordpress.com/2015/04/20/tulip-poplar-a-rich-resource-for-year-round-wilderness-self-reliance/

Noble, Christian (2013), 'The Tinder Bundle', Master Woodsman (inner-tree bark among tinder materials; its featured bundle is tulip tree / yellow poplar inner bark): https://masterwoodsman.com/2013/tinder-bundle/

usnea.name: Old man's beard lichen
usnea.from: Pulled in pale grey-green tufts from the branches of conifers.
usnea.notes: Damp straight off the tree after fog, but it dries fast if carried inside your clothes.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Usnea' ('When dry, Usnea lichens are flammable and can be used as a fire starter'): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Usnea

Missouri Department of Conservation, Field Guide, 'Beard Lichens (Usnea Lichens)' ('When dry, shrubby lichens such as these have been used as tinder for starting fires'; soft, absorbent tissues): https://mdc.mo.gov/discover-nature/field-guide/beard-lichens-usnea-lichens
